transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I... I suppose I came in because things at work have been incredibly stressful lately, and it's starting to really wear me down. I’m a secondary school teacher—I teach history, actually, mostly tenth and eleventh graders—and I’ve been at my current district for a long time. But recently, I just can’t shake this feeling... this very intense, unsettling feeling about the daily communication at the school. 

It started with the morning announcements. The principal gets on the PA system every morning at 8:15, and on the surface, I know it sounds like he’s just talking about cafeteria rules or upcoming assembly schedules, but to me, it feels like there are coded messages hidden in his words, specifically directed at me. And then it started happening with the staff emails, too. We get these regular administrative memos, and the phrasing they use just feels so pointed, like they're trying to send me a hidden message about my life or my job performance through the subtext. 

I’ve tried to rationalize it, I really have. I even confided in one of my colleagues about it—she teaches math right across the hall from me, we've been friends for years—and she was very sweet about it. She actually had me sit down at her desk and she gently pulled up her own laptop to show me her inbox, just to prove that those exact same emails were sent to the entire faculty mailing list. She kept saying, "Look, see? We all got the exact same message, it's just a standard memo." But the thing is, even seeing her screen with my own eyes, even knowing logically that the email went to every single teacher in the building, I still can’t shake the feeling that the true meaning of the message is meant only for me. It’s just exhausting, honestly, trying to decipher what they want from me every single morning before the first bell even rings, and I just don't know how to make it stop.
Can you tell me if these messages you're perceiving feel like something that could possibly be real, or do you sometimes wonder if others don’t interpret them the same way you do?

Well, that's... that's the part that is so incredibly frustrating, doctor. Because, on the one hand, I have eyes and ears, and I've been an educator for over thirty years. I know how mass communication works. When Sarah—that's my friend across the hall, Sarah Jenkins, she's wonderful, she's been there almost as long as I have—when she showed me her screen, I could physically see that the email header said 'All Staff.' I saw the little icon that indicates it went to the entire district server. So, logically, a part of my brain, the rational part that grades papers and plans lesson units, knows that everyone is looking at the exact same text. 

But... but then I actually read the words. Like, last Tuesday, there was a memo about 'streamlining hall pass procedures to maximize instructional time.' And to Sarah, it just meant we need to be stricter about letting kids go to the bathroom. But when I read it, it felt like... like a spotlight was shining directly on me. The word 'streamlining,' the way it was positioned in the sentence, it felt so specifically tied to a conversation I had with a student weeks ago. It felt like the administration was saying, 'We know what you did, and we are watching how you manage your time.' 

So, to answer your question... I know others don't interpret it the same way. Sarah clearly didn't. She just sighed and said, 'More paperwork.' But for me, the feeling that it is a coded message about me is so overwhelming, so physically real in my chest, that it overrides the logic of it being a mass email. It's like... it's like we're all looking at the same painting, but everyone else sees a landscape, and I see a portrait of myself, and I can't convince them to see what I see, but I also can't unsee it. And it's just... it's the same with the morning announcements. The principal will say something about 'maintaining school pride,' and I just know, I feel it in my bones, that he's talking about my lesson on the Civil War from the day before. It's just so real to me, even when the evidence says it shouldn't be.
Have you noticed these kinds of messages or feelings happening outside of school, like in news broadcasts, TV shows, or conversations with people not related to your job?

Well, that’s an interesting question, doctor, because I’ve actually thought a lot about that. I’ve tried to pay very close attention to whether this... this phenomenon, I suppose you could call it, is happening when I’m at home, or when I’m out running errands, or, you know, watching the evening news. I usually watch the local news at 6:00, just to catch up on the weather and local events, and then maybe a documentary or a historical drama later in the evening, given my background in history. I love those Ken Burns series, for instance. 

But to answer your question directly... no, I really haven't noticed it outside of the school environment. When I'm watching the news, the anchor just seems to be reporting the news. If they're talking about a local city council meeting or a traffic accident on the interstate, it just feels like information being broadcast to the public. I don't get that sudden, dropping sensation in my stomach like I do when the principal speaks over the PA system. I don't feel like the newscaster is looking through the screen at me, or embedding some sort of critique of my life into their script. 

And it's the same with conversations outside of work. I go to a book club once a month—we meet at this lovely little coffee shop downtown, mostly women my age, some retired, some still working—and when we discuss the books, even if we get into deep or philosophical topics, I never feel like they are secretly talking about me. Their words just mean what they mean. 

It really seems to be entirely localized to the school district, to the administration, the morning announcements, the staff emails... it's like there's a specific frequency that only broadcasts within the walls of the school building, and only I am tuned into it. When I drive off the school parking lot at the end of the day, it's almost like a physical weight lifts, and the rest of the world—the radio in my car, the cashier at the grocery store, the television in my living room—they all just go back to being normal, straightforward communication. So, no, it hasn't bled into the rest of my life, thank goodness, but that almost makes it more confusing, doesn't it? Why just at work? Why just those specific people?
Have you ever felt that people or events outside of school, like in your personal life or in the media, were also sending you hidden messages or had special meanings specifically for you?

Well, no, not outside of school. I mean, I think I was just saying that, wasn't I? It's really just the school. I... I know I came in today specifically because I just can't shake this feeling that certain staff emails and the morning announcements are really coded messages about me. It's the school environment, the administration. Like I mentioned, even when Sarah—my friend Sarah Jenkins, across the hall, the math teacher—even when she very gently, very sweetly, pulls up her own email to show me that the exact same message was sent to everyone, to the whole staff mailing list... I still feel it. I still feel like the true meaning is directed right at me. 

But out in the world? No. The grocery store, the book club, the Ken Burns documentaries on PBS... none of that feels coded. It's just... it's just the school. The announcements. The memos. It's like the moment I step into the building, there's this heavy, suffocating layer of subtext that only I can read, and it's all about me. And even when people like Sarah try to help, try to show me the logic of it being a mass email... the feeling just doesn't go away. It's just so exhausting, doctor.
Have you ever seen, heard, or sensed things that others around you don’t seem to notice, even outside of these messages you’ve been describing?

Well, now that you ask it that way... I suppose, yes. I haven't really put it in the same box as the emails or the morning announcements, because it doesn't feel like a coded message or a critique, but... yes, there is something else. 

You know how it is at a high school after the final bell rings at 3:15. The hallways are absolute chaos for about twenty minutes—lockers slamming, teenagers shouting across the corridor, the buses revving up outside. But by 4:00 or 4:30, if there aren't any extracurriculars meeting in my wing, the building gets incredibly, almost unnervingly quiet. I usually stay late to grade. I've been doing this a long time, and I just despise bringing stacks of essays home to my dining room table if I can avoid it. So, I'll be sitting there at my desk, completely alone, just me and my red pen, and... I'll hear a voice. 

It's a woman's voice. And it's not a whisper, or a mumble, or something I have to strain to hear. It's perfectly clear. She'll just say my name, or she'll make a very short, casual comment about exactly what I'm doing right then. She might say, 'You've been at that a while,' or 'Almost finished.' And it sounds so natural, so completely normal, that I don't even think to question it. I actually answer her out loud! I'll say something like, 'Just one more paragraph,' or 'I know, I'm wrapping up,' thinking maybe Sarah from across the hall popped her head in, or one of the custodians is emptying the trash. And then I turn my chair around, and... the room is completely empty. The door is still shut. There is absolutely no one there. 

And it’s not just at school, either. It happens in the quiet of my house, too. My house is an older split-level, built in the late seventies, so I'm used to normal house noises, the furnace kicking on, the floorboards settling. But this isn't that. I'll just be in the kitchen, maybe wiping down the counters after dinner or waiting for the kettle to boil for my evening tea—I always have chamomile around 8:00 to help me wind down—and I'll hear her again. Just my name, or a brief little comment. And just like at school, I'll speak right back to her before my brain catches up. I'll say, 'Just a minute!' or 'I'm right here,' to the empty kitchen. And then I just stand there holding the dishcloth, realizing I'm completely alone in the house. It’s... it's very unsettling, doctor, to answer someone so clearly and then realize you're talking to thin air.
When you hear the woman’s voice, are there any actual sounds in the environment that could explain it, like a radio, television, or someone speaking nearby?

Well, I've thought about that, too, because I am a very rational person, doctor. I teach history, I deal in facts and primary sources, so my first instinct is always to look for a logical explanation. I've gone over it in my head so many times, trying to figure out if it's just a trick of the acoustics, you know? Like, is the HVAC system carrying sound from another part of the building? But no, it's not like that. 

When I hear her, it's not muffled or distorted the way it would be if it were coming through a vent or from down the hall. It doesn't sound like a radio left on in the next room, or a television playing in the background. It is so clear and distinct, as if she is standing right next to me, maybe just over my shoulder. That's why I answer her so automatically! If it sounded like a distant echo, I wouldn't say, 'Just a minute!' or 'I'm almost finished grading.' I only answer because it sounds like a real person, right there in the room with me. 

And it's the exact same way at home. I mean, my house is quiet. I live alone, I don't leave the television on for background noise—I find it too distracting when I'm trying to unwind or read. So when I'm in the kitchen making my tea, there isn't a radio on, there isn't a TV on, the windows are usually closed... there is absolutely nothing that could be mistaken for a woman speaking directly to me. It's just the quiet of the house, and then, suddenly, her voice. It's so vivid that my brain just registers it as a person speaking to me, plain as day, before I have the chance to realize that it's impossible because I'm the only one there. It’s not a misheard noise, doctor. It’s a voice, clear as a bell, coming from nowhere.
Have you ever had beliefs or experiences, outside of the school environment, where you felt things had special meanings or were connected to you in ways others didn’t understand?

Well, doctor, I... I feel like we might be going in circles just a little bit here. Because, like I said when we first started talking, no. It’s really not outside of the school. I don't go to the supermarket or watch the local news and think anyone is trying to send me a signal. My life outside of work is very quiet, very ordinary.

But the feeling just sits there, heavy in my chest. I still read the email and feel, absolutely down to my bones, that the subtext is directed solely at me. It's like everyone else is reading a generic memo about dress codes or assembly schedules, and I'm reading a personal, hidden critique. 

So, to answer your question again, no, it’s not outside the school. It is entirely tied to the building and those specific messages. I just don't understand why my brain won't let it go even when Sarah shows me the proof. It’s just so exhausting to deal with every single morning.

And again, while it is certainly startling to find myself answering an empty room, it really isn't the thing that is consuming my life right now. I just keep hoping we can get back to the actual issue with the administration and those staff emails, because that is the situation that is making my job impossible, and that is what I really need to figure out today.

inference.note: F22 (Persistent delusional disorder) is ruled out as the patient's delusional experiences are more pervasive and not limited to a single theme over a long period without deterioration of functioning. Auditory hallucinations and the presence of multiple delusional themes (coded messages in emails/announcements) support schizophrenia (F20) or schizoaffective disorder (F25).

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences the auditory hallucinations in the absence of any external stimuli, confirming if they occur in situations where no real person could be present.
doctor.question: Have you ever heard the woman’s voice when you were absolutely certain that you were completely alone and there was no possibility of someone actually being nearby, such as when all the doors were closed or you were in a locked room?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes in the quiet of my house or after the classroom empties, I hear a woman’s voice say my name or make a short comment about what I’m doing, clear enough that I answer before realizing no one is there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the context in which I hear the woman's voice (when I am completely alone), which relates directly to my auditory hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I really don't mean to be difficult, but I feel like I am repeating myself over and over, and we are just spinning our wheels here. Yes, of course I am alone. That is exactly what I have been trying to tell you this entire time. 

It is always when I am completely, utterly alone. Like I said, it happens after the final bell has rung, the kids have all rushed out to the buses, my colleagues have packed up and gone home, and I am the only person left in that entire wing of the building. The door to my classroom will be shut. Or, like I also mentioned, it happens when I am at home, in the evening, when the house is completely locked up for the night and it is just absolutely quiet. 

I will be in that complete isolation, doing something incredibly boring—grading papers, wiping down the counters, just going about my business—and then, out of nowhere, I hear her. She will just say my first name, or she will make a very quick, short comment about exactly what I am doing right in that moment. And it is so clear, so incredibly distinct and real, that I don't even think about the fact that the doors are locked or that I am the only one in the building. My immediate, gut reaction is just to answer her. I will literally say, out loud, 'Just a minute,' or 'Yes?' 

It is only after the words leave my mouth that my brain catches up and I remember, 'Wait, the door is locked. I am the only one here.' I look around, and of course, the room is completely empty. There is no possibility of anyone being there. 

So, yes, it happens when I am absolutely certain I am alone. But Doctor, please, I have explained this voice from every possible angle now. It is startling, yes, but it is just a brief moment in my day. It is not the thing that is keeping me up at night. What is keeping me up at night, what is making it so incredibly difficult to just walk into the staff room or open my inbox every morning, is the administration and those emails. I really, really need us to focus on that, because I feel like we are wasting time on these locked doors when my actual career feels like it is on the line. Can we please talk about the emails now?

The delusions are non-bizarre, circumscribed to the school environment, and present for months, fulfilling criteria for paranoid-type schizophrenia. Schizoaffective disorder is considered but ruled out due to lack of major mood episodes.
